The natural person, apart from the Father's drawing, cannot come to Christ. “Draws” (helkō) means to pull with force — the same word used in 21:6 for hauling in a net full of fish. This is not gentle persuasion but sovereign action that overcomes the resistance of the human will. The drawing and the raising on the last day are linked: the Father who draws is the same one who guarantees the final resurrection of all he gives to the Son (v. 39).

verseByVerse.quote: It is written in the Prophets, 'And they will all be taught by God.' Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me... I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever.
verseByVerse.commentary: The citation of Isaiah 54:13 — they will all be taught by God — grounds the coming to Jesus in prior divine work: those who come to Jesus have been taught by the Father, drawn by the Father, given by the Father. The Father's teaching is not an external instruction but an internal renewal of the heart that creates the desire and capacity to come. Jesus's claim to be the living bread that came down from heaven — distinguished from the manna that their fathers ate and died — escalates the comparison with Moses: Moses gave bread that sustained biological life temporarily; Jesus gives bread that produces eternal life. The bread Jesus gives is his flesh, which anticipates both the Eucharist and the atonement: the living bread is given through death, and eating it means receiving the life that his death purchases.

verseByVerse.quote: “The bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The most scandalous statement in the discourse. “Eating his flesh and drinking his blood” is not primarily Eucharistic language (though the Lord's Supper is its sacramental enactment) — it is the language of radical, personal faith-union with the crucified Christ. To eat his flesh is to feed on the reality of his incarnation and death; to drink his blood is to receive the life poured out at the cross. The offence is deliberate: Jesus will not allow his hearers to have him on their own terms. He must be eaten — ingested, internalized, depended on completely. Those who refuse find the saying “hard” (v. 60). Those who receive it find eternal life.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, 'How can this man give us his flesh to eat?'... After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The escalation from eating the bread to eating the flesh and drinking the blood (vv.53-58) is the point at which Jesus's teaching becomes most offensive: drinking blood violated a fundamental Jewish prohibition, and the language of eating flesh echoed nothing in the tradition that could make it acceptable. The offence is deliberate: Jesus is pressing the question of his identity to the point where no neutral response is possible. His clarification — it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all; the words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life (v.63) — suggests that the eating and drinking are spiritual realities, received by faith in Jesus's words, not a physical cannibalism. The departure of the many disciples — this is a hard saying; who can listen to it? — is John's great tragic moment: the crowds who followed for the loaves will not follow for the cross. Peter's response to Jesus's question — to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life — is the definition of discipleship: not understanding everything, but having nowhere else to go.

verseByVerse.quote: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's confession at the end of chapter 6 is the Johannine equivalent of Caesarea Philippi (Matt 16). It is faith in the dark — many disciples have just left (v. 66), the discourse has been hard, Jesus has asked “Do you want to go away as well?” (v. 67). Peter's answer is not triumphant certainty but the confession of a man who has no better option: nowhere else to go, and knowing it. This is the purest form of faith: not faith based on full understanding, not faith based on comfortable circumstances, but faith in a person because there is simply no one else. “You have the words of eternal life” — wherever those words take us, we must follow.

6.theology: Effectual grace and the perseverance of the saints. John 6 contains the strongest concentration of Calvinist soteriology in the Gospels. The Father gives specific people to the Son (v. 37, 39); the Son loses none of them (v. 39); they will all be raised on the last day (v. 40, 44, 54). This is the chain of salvation: divine election (the Father's giving), effectual drawing (v. 44), present possession of eternal life (v. 54), and final resurrection (v. 54). The perseverance of the saints is not based on the strength of the believer's grip on Christ but on the strength of Christ's grip on the believer: “I will raise him up on the last day” — the action is Christ's, not the believer's. Those who truly come to the Son will never be cast out (v. 37).
6.examples:
Then: The crowd that was fed in the wilderness followed Jesus to Capernaum seeking more bread. When he gave them himself instead, most left. They wanted the kingdom's benefits without the King himself. The same choice faces every hearer of the gospel: receive Christ on his own terms, or turn away to find something more manageable.

Now: Peter's question — “To whom shall we go?” — is the right question for every moment of doubt, difficulty, or disillusionment in the Christian life. Not “is the doctrine correct?” but “is there anyone else?” The answer is always the same: he alone has the words of eternal life. The bread of life is not comfortable or easy; he is necessary. And what is necessary for life, when truly seen, becomes the object of desire.

7.title: Rivers of Living Water
7.text: <sup>37</sup>On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. <sup>38</sup>Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'” <sup>39</sup>(He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.) <sup>40</sup>When they heard these words, some of the people said, “This really is the Prophet.” <sup>41</sup>Others said, “This is the Christ.” But some said, “Is the Christ to come from Galilee?” <sup>45</sup>The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, “Why did you not bring him?” <sup>46</sup>The officers answered, “No one ever spoke like this man!”
7.overview:
Chapter 7 takes place at the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkoth) — the great autumn harvest festival when Israel camped in booths and celebrated the wilderness years, the water that God provided, and the anticipated coming of the Spirit at the end of the age. Every day of the feast a priest carried water from the pool of Siloam and poured it on the altar while the people sang Psalm 118. On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood up and cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” He claims to be the fulfilment of everything the feast anticipated.

The chapter is dominated by division: the crowds are divided about Jesus (vv. 40–43); the religious authorities are divided (Nicodemus speaks up in his defence, v. 50–51); even the temple police are disarmed by him (“No one ever spoke like this man!”). Division (schisma) is the inevitable result of the arrival of light in a dark world: those who love the light come to it; those who love the darkness retreat from it.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Now the Jews' Feast of Tabernacles was at hand... Jesus went up to the temple and began teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Feast of Tabernacles is the interpretive key to John 7-8: the eight-day feast celebrated Israel's wilderness sojourn, included water-pouring rituals at the Siloam pool, and was associated with eschatological themes (Zech 14:16-21). Jesus's brothers' advice — show yourself to the world — misunderstands his mission as a public campaign; Jesus's response — my time has not yet come — maintains the Father's control over the timetable. His secret journey to Jerusalem and his public teaching in the temple creates a pattern of divine hiddenness and disclosure that runs through both chapters: he is always partially revealed, never fully comprehended. The crowd's divided opinion — some say he is a good man, others say he is leading the people astray — is John's consistent depiction of Jesus's reception: his words always divide, always demand a verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: At that point some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, 'Is not this the man whom they seek to kill? And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?'
verseByVerse.commentary: The Jerusalemites' puzzlement — why is no one arresting this man? — and the crowd's theological objection — when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from — reveal multiple layers of misunderstanding. They think Jesus's origin is known (Galilee, Nazareth) but the Christ's is unknown; Jesus's response is that they know where he is from in the earthly sense but not in the heavenly sense — he is from the Father who sent him, whom they do not know. The attempt to arrest Jesus that fails (his hour had not yet come) and the Pharisees' dispatch of officers to arrest him sets up the dramatic scene of verses 45-52, where the officers return empty-handed, explaining that no one ever spoke like this man. The temple police have encountered something they cannot categorise: a man whose words have a quality that no legal instrument can touch.

verseByVerse.quote: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The setting is the last day of Tabernacles, the climax of the water-pouring ceremony. At the very moment Israel celebrates God's provision of water in the wilderness and prays for the Spirit to be poured out in the last days (Isa 44:3; Joel 2:28), Jesus claims to be the source of that water. “Come to me and drink” — the same universal invitation as Isaiah 55:1, now embodied in a person. The rivers of living water flowing from the believer (v. 38) are the overflow of the Spirit received through faith in Christ. The gift of the Spirit is the immediate consequence and evidence of believing in the glorified Son.

verseByVerse.quote: (He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.)
verseByVerse.commentary: John's parenthetical comment is theologically crucial. The giving of the Spirit awaits the glorification of Jesus — which in John means the cross, resurrection, and ascension together. The Spirit cannot be poured out in his fullness until the redemption is accomplished, the risen Christ is enthroned, and the new covenant age is inaugurated at Pentecost. The Paraclete — the Helper, the Spirit of truth — is the gift of the glorified Son to his people, and his coming is the experiential realization of everything the Tabernacles feast anticipated.

verseByVerse.quote: “This really is the Prophet.” Others said, “This is the Christ.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The crowd's divided responses map the range of messianic expectation in first-century Judaism. “The Prophet” refers to the figure of Deuteronomy 18:15 — the prophet like Moses who would come to speak God's definitive word. “The Christ” refers to the Davidic king. Jesus is both — and more than both. The objection about Galilee (v. 41) is based on ignorance of his Bethlehem birth. The theological point stands: no human category is adequate for Jesus. He is the eternal Word, the Son of God, who can only be named adequately from within the Trinitarian life.

verseByVerse.quote: Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was? So there was a division among the people over him. Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The crowd's Scriptural objection about Bethlehem is one of John's rich ironies: they think they are disqualifying Jesus, but the reader knows (from Matthew and Luke) that Jesus was in fact born in Bethlehem — the objection is based on a factual error. John does not correct it; he lets the irony stand, because the deeper point is that those who are arguing about Bethlehem versus Galilee are arguing about the letter of a prophecy while missing the person the prophecy is about. The officers' return to the Pharisees without having arrested Jesus (v.45) provokes the question: why? No one ever spoke like this man — the explanation that even law-enforcement officers could not resist. The Pharisees' contemptuous response — this crowd that does not know the law is accursed — reveals the condescension of the religious establishment toward those who are responding to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: “No one ever spoke like this man!”
verseByVerse.commentary: The temple police sent to arrest Jesus return empty-handed, undone by his words. Their testimony is an inadvertent confession: the authority, the clarity, the depth, the love in his teaching were unlike anything they had ever heard. This is the consistent testimony of all who encounter the teaching of Jesus honestly: “the crowds were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority” (Matt 7:28–29). The words of Jesus have this effect not merely because they are intellectually brilliant but because they carry the weight of the one who speaks them. When the eternal Word speaks human language, human language is used beyond its natural capacity.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees answered them, 'Have you also been deceived? Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him? But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The Pharisees' contempt for the crowd — accursed because ignorant of the law — is the irony John has been building toward: the supposed guardians of the law are the ones who have most thoroughly misread it, while the common people are recognising in Jesus what the law promised. Nicodemus's intervention — does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing? — is the only Pharisee in the council who applies the law correctly (Deut 1:16-17; 19:15), and his question is dismissed with contempt. The question put back to him — search and see: no prophet arises from Galilee — is wrong twice: the law does not require Galilean origin to disqualify prophets, and Jonah (2 Kings 14:25) was from Gath-hepher, which is in Galilee. The dismissiveness of the ruling class that prides itself on legal knowledge is itself an ironic demonstration of their ignorance.

verseByVerse.quote: “Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing?”
verseByVerse.commentary: Nicodemus, who came to Jesus by night in chapter 3, now speaks up — cautiously, juridically, without naming his sympathy. It is a small act of courage in a hostile room, and it costs him the scorn of his colleagues (v. 52). He is making his way, slowly, from the dark to the light. His eventual emergence at the burial (19:39) shows that the seed planted at the night conversation has been growing. John traces his journey across the Gospel as a pastoral model: coming to faith is often a slow walk through objection, partial commitment, gradual illumination. The Spirit moves at his own pace in each life.

7.theology: The Holy Spirit as the gift of the glorified Christ. John 7:39 establishes the Trinitarian and redemptive-historical logic of Pentecost. The Spirit is not given independently of the Son's atoning work; he is the gift of the glorified Christ, the experiential realization of the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36. Reformed theology has always insisted that the Spirit's work is Christ-centred: he does not draw attention to himself but to the Son (16:14 — “he will glorify me”). The rivers of living water flowing from the believer are not the product of a second blessing or a special experience; they are the ordinary fruit of union with the glorified Christ through faith. Every believer who has received the Spirit has received the fullness of the promise — and the river runs to eternal life.
7.examples:
Then: The Feast of Tabernacles was the most joyful feast in Israel's calendar — eight days of celebration, lights, water, music, the memory of the wilderness and the anticipation of the age to come. Jesus chose this moment to make his most public claim. The timing was not coincidental; the feast was the sign, and he was the substance. Every joy the feast evoked was a pointer to the joy that flows from knowing him.

Now: “No one ever spoke like this man.” The words of Jesus retain their authority across every century and every culture. When the Gospel is preached faithfully, the same astonishment is still possible — not because of the preacher's eloquence but because the words carry the weight of the one who first spoke them. The living water he promised on the last day of Tabernacles is still flowing. The thirsty are still invited to come and drink.

8.title: The Light of the World
8.text: <sup>12</sup>Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” <sup>23</sup>He said to them, “You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. <sup>24</sup>I told you that you would die in your sins, for unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins.” <sup>31</sup>So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, “If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, <sup>32</sup>and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” <sup>36</sup>So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed. <sup>44</sup>You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. <sup>56</sup>Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad.” <sup>57</sup>So the Jews said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” <sup>58</sup>Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.” <sup>59</sup>So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is the most theologically explosive chapter in John thus far. It opens during the Feast of Tabernacles — when the temple courts were lit with enormous golden menorahs, filling the night sky with light — and Jesus announces: “I am the light of the world.” The second “I AM” statement takes the feast’s imagery and turns it into a self-declaration. He is what the torches anticipated. Every page of the chapter drives toward the climax: “Before Abraham was, I AM” — the unambiguous appropriation of the divine name of Exodus 3:14, spoken in the precincts of the Jerusalem temple. His hearers pick up stones. They know exactly what he means.

Between the second and the seventh “I AM” statements comes a searching discourse on freedom, truth, slavery, and the devil. Jesus diagnoses his opponents’ spiritual condition with surgical precision: they are slaves to sin, children of the devil, unable to hear his word because they have no place in their hearts for the truth. The only liberation is the truth — which is not a set of propositions but a person: “the truth will set you free,” and “if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” Freedom in John is not autonomy from God; it is liberation from sin’s tyranny, which comes only through union with the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Early in the morning he came again to the temple... The scribes and Pharisees brought a woman who had been caught in adultery... 'Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery. Now in the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. So what do you say?'
verseByVerse.commentary: The pericope adulterae (vv.1-11) has a complex textual history — it is absent from the earliest manuscripts and almost certainly was not part of John's original text — but its content is entirely consistent with the character of Jesus shown throughout the Gospels: he does not condone the sin, he does not participate in the entrapment, and he offers the woman dignity and the opportunity for a new beginning. The scribes and Pharisees bring the woman as a trap: if Jesus says stone her, he violates Roman law (Jews could not carry out capital punishment) and loses his reputation for mercy; if he says release her, he violates Mosaic law and loses his authority. Jesus's writing on the ground, his challenge — let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone — and the accusers' departure one by one, oldest first, is one of the most dramatically precise episodes in the Gospel tradition. His closing word — neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more — combines the grace that does not condemn with the holiness that calls to a transformed life.

verseByVerse.quote: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The second “I AM” statement. The Feast of Tabernacles involved the lighting of four great menorahs in the Court of Women, whose light illuminated all Jerusalem — a reminder of the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness. Jesus stands in those courts and claims to be the light that the pillars of fire, the Shekinah glory, and the menorahs all pointed to. “The light of life” — a phrase from Psalm 56:13 — means both the light that gives life and the life that is itself light. To follow Jesus is to walk in the light that dispels not only physical but moral, spiritual, and eternal darkness.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Pharisees said to him, 'You are bearing witness about yourself; your testimony is not true.' Jesus answered, 'Even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from and where I am going.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The dispute about testimony continues the legal metaphor of John 5: witness, judgment, truth. Jesus's claim that his self-testimony is true because he knows his origin and destination is not circular reasoning but a claim about unique epistemic access: only Jesus knows where he came from (the Father's bosom, 1:18) and where he is going (back to the Father, 13:3). His announcement that he will go away and they will seek him and not find him, and that where he is going they cannot come, is met with misunderstanding (suicide?) that John uses to deepen the theological point: the division between above and below, not between the living and the dead, is what separates Jesus from his opponents. The I AM sayings of verses 24 and 28 — unless you believe that I AM, you will die in your sins — make explicit that the name of God (Exod 3:14) is at stake in the question of Jesus's identity.

verseByVerse.quote: “You will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The most famous verse in chapter 8 is habitually quoted out of context. “The truth” is not abstract philosophical truth or scientific fact but the revelation of God in Jesus himself (14:6 — “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”). “Will set you free” — free from what? Verse 34 defines it: from sin. The freedom Jesus offers is not political liberation (which his hearers desire) or philosophical enlightenment (which the Hellenistic world desires) but emancipation from the tyranny of sin and the condemnation it brings. “If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” — free in reality, not merely in status. The freedom is as deep as the slavery was.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, 'We are offspring of Abraham and have never been enslaved to anyone. How is it that you say, You will become free?' Jesus answered them, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin. The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The claim never to have been enslaved is historically remarkable (Egypt! Babylon! Rome!) and reveals the nature of the blindness Jesus is diagnosing: they cannot see their actual condition because their self-understanding is shaped by a narrative of freedom (Abraham's descendants) rather than the reality of bondage (to sin). Jesus's distinction between slave and son in the household is a social reality with theological weight: the slave's tenure is contingent; the son's is permanent. The freedom that the Son gives — if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed — is the freedom of those who participate in the Son's own relationship to the Father, the permanent status of the children of God rather than the conditional status of household servants.

verseByVerse.quote: I know that you are offspring of Abraham; yet you seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you. I speak of what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have heard from your father.
verseByVerse.commentary: The parallel between Jesus and the Father, and between the opponents and their father, is developing toward the climax of verse 44. Jesus acknowledges their physical descent from Abraham while denying their spiritual kinship: the children of Abraham do the works of Abraham, which means they would receive and welcome God's messenger. Their desire to kill Jesus is proof that another paternity is operative. The contrast between seeing (Jesus has seen the Father) and hearing (they have heard their father) establishes the epistemological basis for the dispute: Jesus speaks from direct knowledge of the Father; they act from what they have received from an alternative source. The opponents' claim to God as their father is dismissed: if God were your Father, you would love me — the test of paternity is recognition and love of the Father's Son.

verseByVerse.quote: “You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father’s desires.”
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the most severe word Jesus speaks to anyone in John’s Gospel. He is not characterising his opponents as morally worse than others — he is diagnosing their spiritual paternity. To be “of the devil” is to share his fundamental orientation: away from truth, toward murder and deceit. The devil is the father of lies (v. 44) because he introduced the first lie in the garden (Gen 3:4). Those who reject the truth about Jesus align themselves, whether they know it or not, with the one who has been lying from the beginning. This is not ethnic slander; it is spiritual diagnosis. The remedy is available: “if you abide in my word… the truth will set you free.”

verseByVerse.quote: But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me. Which one of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me? Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason why you do not hear them is that you are not of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus's challenge — which one of you convicts me of sin? — is an invitation to examine him by their own standard, and it goes unanswered because no charge can be sustained. The inability to convict him is itself an argument for the truth of his claims: if his life is consistent with his words, the words should be trusted. The dialogue escalates: they call him a Samaritan and demon-possessed; he responds by claiming to honour the Father and by making the astonishing statement that whoever keeps his word will never see death. Their counter — now we know you have a demon, Abraham died and so did the prophets — tries to bring him back within human categories where his claim is obviously false. Jesus's response — before Abraham was, I AM — is the most explicit claim to pre-existence and divine identity in the entire Gospel, and its effect is immediate: they take up stones to throw at him.

verseByVerse.quote: “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus makes an extraordinary claim: Abraham anticipated and rejoiced in the coming of Christ. The precise reference is debated — possibly the birth of Isaac (a type of the promised Son), possibly Abraham’s vision in Genesis 15 — but the theological point is clear: the entire history of Israel was oriented toward the one who now stands before them. Abraham is not Jesus’ ancestor in the ordinary sense; Jesus is the one in whom the Abrahamic covenant finds its fulfilment and its goal. The opponents’ appeal to Abraham as their father is answered by Jesus’ revelation that Abraham was waiting for him.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to him, 'You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?' Jesus said to them, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I AM.' So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary: The ego eimi of verse 58 — before Abraham was, I AM — is the culmination of John's I AM sayings without a predicate: not I am the bread, or I am the light, but simply I AM, the unqualified divine name of Exodus 3:14. The crowd's reaction — picking up stones — is the correct response to genuine blasphemy if the claim were false; it is also the tragic response to a correct claim that surpasses their theological imagination. Jesus's escape (he hid himself) continues the pattern of divine control over the timing of his passion: the hour had not yet come, and so the stones find no target. John 8 ends where it began, at the temple, but everything has changed: Jesus has claimed the divine name, offered freedom from sin's slavery, and identified the ultimate issue as paternity — whose children are we? The answer determines everything.

verseByVerse.quote: “Before Abraham was, I am.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The most audacious claim in the Gospel before the resurrection. The grammar is deliberately jarring: “before Abraham was” (aorist — a completed past event) contrasted with “I am” (present tense, continuous existence). He does not say “I was before Abraham” (which would merely assert pre-existence). He says “I AM” — the divine name of Exodus 3:14, the eternal self-existence of God. His opponents understand perfectly: they reach for stones (v. 59), the penalty for blasphemy. Jesus is not correcting them for misunderstanding; he is escaping them because his hour has not yet come. He has claimed to be Yahweh. Everything else in the Gospel follows from this claim.

8.theology: The divine “I AM” and the nature of Christ’s deity. The “Before Abraham was, I AM” of John 8:58 is the strongest Christological claim in the Synoptic or Johannine tradition. It is not a claim to pre-existence in the sense of existing before birth (as angels do); it is a claim to the eternal, self-existent being that belongs to God alone. The name “I AM” (Heb. YHWH; Greek ego eimi) is the name that cannot be given to a creature — it names the one who simply IS, who derives existence from no source outside himself, who was never not. Jesus claims this name for himself. The response of the Pharisees (picking up stones) is theologically correct; if he is not who he says he is, it is blasphemy. If he is, it is the most important moment in human history.
8.examples:
Then: The chapter opens with the account of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11, textually disputed but ancient and consistent with Jesus’ character). Jesus neither condemns nor excuses; he forgives and commands: “Go, and from now on sin no more.” The one who is the light of the world is also the one who does not condemn those who come to him in their darkness. Both truths belong together: the holiness that says “sin no more” and the mercy that says “neither do I condemn you.”

Now: “The truth will set you free” has become a cultural slogan stripped of its content. Universities inscribe it on their gates meaning intellectual liberation; political movements appropriate it for their causes. But in John 8, the freedom is specific: freedom from sin, from the devil’s dominion, from the condemnation that hangs over every human being apart from grace. Only the Son can give this freedom — and he gives it freely to all who abide in his word.

9.title: The Man Born Blind
9.text: <sup>1</sup>As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. <sup>2</sup>And his disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” <sup>3</sup>Jesus answered, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. <sup>6</sup>Having said these things, he spat on the ground and made mud with the saliva. Then he anointed the man’s eyes with the mud <sup>7</sup>and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam.” So he went and washed and came back seeing. <sup>17</sup>So they said again to the blind man, “What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes?” He said, “He is a prophet.” <sup>35</sup>Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?” <sup>36</sup>He answered, “And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?” <sup>37</sup>Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you.” <sup>38</sup>He said, “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped him. <sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the most dramatically structured chapter in John. It tells the story of a man who begins blind and ends worshipping; a story of Pharisees who begin certain they can see and end in declared blindness. The healing of the man born blind — the sixth sign — is simultaneously a physical miracle and a parable of the entire Gospel: Jesus is the light of the world (8:12), and his coming forces a division between those who receive the light and those who refuse it.

John narrates the story in a series of scenes that trace the man’s progressive confession: “The man called Jesus” (v. 11) → “He is a prophet” (v. 17) → “If this man were not from God, he could do nothing” (v. 33) → “Lord, I believe” (v. 38). Meanwhile the Pharisees move in the opposite direction: initial investigation → division → expulsion of the man → declared blindness (v. 41). The chapter is a masterpiece of literary irony: those who claim to see are blind; the one who was born blind ends by seeing — and by worshipping the Son of God. This is John’s picture of conversion and of the world’s rejection of the light.

verseByVerse.quote: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The passive formulation — he saw — is theologically charged in John's Gospel, where seeing and blindness carry the weight of the chapter's entire argument. Jesus sees the man that others pass by; he sees him specifically, as the object of a sign that will display the works of God. The blind man has been blind from birth, which is emphasised four times in this chapter: his blindness is congenital, total, and beyond any human remedy. He represents not just a man with a disability but the human condition before the light of the world arrives — born without the sight that the Creator intended, dependent on a work of God to receive it. The disciples' theological question about whose sin caused the blindness shows that they too are operating in a system of explanation rather than a posture of compassion: Jesus's response redirects them from analysis to action.

verseByVerse.quote: “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples’ question assumes a direct link between suffering and personal sin — a common assumption in the ancient world, rooted in a misreading of the covenant curses. Jesus does not endorse the link; he breaks it. This man’s blindness is not punishment; it is the occasion for the display of divine glory. This does not mean all suffering is purposeful in this immediate sense — Jesus is making a specific point about this specific man’s situation. But it does mean that the question “whose sin caused this?” is often the wrong question. The better question is “how might God be glorified in this?” That is the question that opens the way for the light to work.

verseByVerse.quote: We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work. As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus's statement about working while it is day — night is coming — is a reference to his approaching death, which will temporarily end his earthly ministry of signs. The urgency is not anxiety but the focused energy of one who knows his appointment: the Father's will has given him specific works to do in a specific time, and the time is limited. The claim I am the light of the world (repeated from 8:12 but now demonstrated in a sign) is enacted in the healing that follows: the man born blind will see; the Pharisees who prided themselves on seeing will be revealed as blind. The sign is a parable: physical blindness healed by Jesus's initiative becomes the story of spiritual blindness healed by the same sovereign grace.

verseByVerse.quote: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam.” So he went and washed and came back seeing.
verseByVerse.commentary: The method is deliberately earthy: mud made with saliva, anointed on the eyes, washed in a specific pool. Jesus does not heal with a word alone (though he could). He uses means — physical, creaturely means — to accomplish a supernatural end. This is the sacramental logic of Christian ministry: the Spirit works through the ordinary (word, water, bread, wine) to accomplish the extraordinary. The pool of Siloam is the pool from which the water was drawn at the Feast of Tabernacles — whose water Jesus claimed to be in chapter 7. The man washes in the waters of the one who is the living water and comes back seeing. He goes in blind and comes back a witness.

verseByVerse.quote: The neighbours and those who had seen him before as a beggar were saying, 'Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?' Some said, 'It is he.' Others said, 'No, but he is like him.' He kept saying, 'I am the man.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The confusion of the neighbours about the healed man's identity — some said it is him, others said it is someone like him — is resolved by the man's own insistence: I am the man. His simplicity is part of his characterisation: he does not know who healed him, he does not know where the healer went, but he knows what happened to him and he states it clearly. The Pharisees' examination reveals their presupposition: this man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath. The division among the Pharisees — some said he is not from God; others said, how can a man who is a sinner do such signs? — shows that the sign is creating the same crisis of division that all of Jesus's signs produce. The man's expanding understanding of Jesus — prophet (v.17), from God (v.33), Lord, I believe (v.38) — is John's model of how encounter with Jesus produces growing recognition.

verseByVerse.quote: “He is a prophet.” / “If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The healed man’s progressive testimony is one of the most moving in the Gospels. He begins with the cautious “he is a prophet” and moves, under sustained interrogation, to the bold declaration: “If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.” He is reasoning from the sign to the one who performed it — exactly what John intends every reader to do. The Pharisees, by contrast, reason from their theological presuppositions (he broke the Sabbath, therefore he cannot be from God) and are unable to receive the evidence before their eyes. The healed man is the model exegete of signs: he lets the evidence lead him to the person.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received his sight... His parents said these things because they feared the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess Jesus to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue.
verseByVerse.commentary: The interrogation of the healed man and his parents is one of the most sustained pieces of narrative irony in John's Gospel. The authorities who are supposed to know the truth keep refusing to accept it; the man who was born blind keeps seeing more clearly. His parents' fear — they feared the Jews because of the synagogue ban — represents the pressure that institutional religion exerts on personal testimony: the threat of excommunication is powerful enough to silence those who know the truth. The man's second interrogation produces his greatest moment: whether he is a sinner I do not know; one thing I do know: I was blind, now I see. This is the purest apologetic — not philosophical argument but the unreasable testimony of personal experience. His escalating boldness — his final question, do you also want to become his disciples? — leads to his ejection from the synagogue, which leads to his meeting with Jesus and his worship.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, 'You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?' And they cast him out... Jesus said, 'For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.' Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, 'Are we also blind?'
verseByVerse.commentary: The Pharisees' ejection of the healed man — you were born in utter sin — applies to him the very theological framework that Jesus had rejected at the chapter's beginning (vv.2-3): his blindness was the result of sin. Having clung to this explanation throughout the chapter, they use it to dismiss both the man and his testimony. Jesus's subsequent meeting with the ejected man, his revelation of himself as the Son of Man, and the man's worship, completes the chapter's movement: the one cast out of the synagogue enters the presence of the Lord. Jesus's judgment-saying — those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind — and the Pharisees' self-incriminating question (are we also blind?) brings the chapter to its theological conclusion: the one who knows his blindness can receive sight; the one who claims to see while remaining spiritually blind bears the full weight of his guilt.

verseByVerse.quote: “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The climax of the chapter. After being cast out of the synagogue — losing his community, his religious standing, his social security — the man is found by Jesus. The Shepherd goes after the one who has been expelled. Jesus reveals himself as the Son of Man, and the man’s response is immediate: “Lord, I believe,” and he worships him. This is saving faith in its simplest form: the revelation of who Jesus is received with trust and responded to with worship. He does not yet have a complete theology; he has an encounter. The encounter is sufficient. Faith is not the accumulation of doctrinal knowledge; it is the reception of the person of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: “That those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The closing irony is devastating. The Pharisees ask sarcastically: “Are we also blind?” Jesus answers: if you were blind (i.e., aware of your inability to see), you would have no guilt — the light would come and heal you. But because you say “We see” — because you are confident in your own spiritual perception — your sin remains. Pride in one’s spiritual sight is the surest evidence of spiritual blindness. This is the consistent teaching of Isaiah 6 (quoted in John 12:40) and of Paul (1 Cor 1:18–25): the gospel is foolishness to those who are wise in their own eyes, and revelation to those who know they cannot see. Blessed are those who mourn their blindness; they will be given sight.

9.theology: Light, blindness, and the irresistible grace of revelation. Chapter 9 enacts what Jesus declared in chapter 8: “I am the light of the world.” The man born blind represents humanity in its natural state — not merely morally deficient but structurally unable to perceive the light of the knowledge of God. The healing is a sovereign act: Jesus acts first, the man does not request healing, he simply obeys the command to go and wash. This is the logic of regeneration: the Spirit illumines first, and the illumined person then believes. The Pharisees’ blindness is the equal and opposite case: those who trust their own spiritual perception cannot receive the light, because they are not looking for it. The chapter is the sixth sign — and like all John’s signs, it calls the reader to examine their own sight: do you see? Or are you, like the Pharisees, confident that you can see when you cannot?
9.examples:
Then: The healed man is cast out of the synagogue — the ancient equivalent of excommunication, social death, economic vulnerability. He loses everything when he tells the truth about Jesus. And then Jesus comes to find him. The one who costs everything is also the one who gives everything back — and more. “Lord, I believe” is spoken by a man who has just lost his entire social world, and it is the freest sentence he has ever spoken.

Now: The question “who sinned?” is still the first instinct when suffering arrives. Parents ask it about disabled children; cancer patients ask it about themselves; churches have been known to imply it about those who suffer. Jesus’ answer remains: stop looking for the guilt and start looking for the glory. The works of God are displayed in the broken places. The light shines most visibly in the deepest darkness.

10.title: The Good Shepherd
10.text: <sup>7</sup>So Jesus again said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. <sup>9</sup>I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture. <sup>11</sup>I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. <sup>14</sup>I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me, <sup>15</sup>just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep. <sup>27</sup>My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. <sup>28</sup>I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. <sup>29</sup>My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand. <sup>30</sup>I and the Father are one.” <sup>38</sup>“even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”
10.overview:
Chapter 10 continues directly from chapter 9 — Jesus addresses those who cast out the healed man, who are the false shepherds of Israel. The good shepherd discourse is the most pastorally rich passage in John’s Gospel and one of the most beloved in all of Scripture. Against the background of Ezekiel 34 (God’s indictment of Israel’s false shepherds and his promise to come himself as the true Shepherd), Jesus announces: “I am the good shepherd.”

The chapter gives us two of the seven “I AM” statements: “I am the door” (v. 7, 9) and “I am the good shepherd” (v. 11, 14). As the door, he is the only legitimate access to the Father’s flock — salvation comes through him alone, and he gives the sheep freedom (“go in and out and find pasture”). As the good shepherd, he knows his sheep by name, calls them, leads them, and lays down his life for them. The chapter climaxes in the most explicit statement of the eternal security of believers in John: “no one will snatch them out of my hand… no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand.” And then: “I and the Father are one” — the clearest statement of divine unity in the Gospel. His opponents again reach for stones.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber. But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary: The parable of the sheepfold opens John 10 in direct continuity with chapter 9: the Jewish authorities who ejected the healed man are the ones Jesus is now addressing with the image of those who enter the sheepfold by climbing rather than by the door. The distinction between the legitimate shepherd and the thief is about authority and purpose: the shepherd enters by the door (legitimate access), is known by the doorkeeper, calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out. The thief comes to steal, kill, and destroy (v.10). Jesus's audience does not understand the parable (v.6), prompting the two I AM interpretations that follow: I am the door (vv.7-9) and I am the good shepherd (vv.11-18). The parable is doing what John's signs do: creating two levels of meaning that require the hearer to decide which world they inhabit.

verseByVerse.quote: “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The third “I AM” statement. In first-century Palestine, a shepherd would lie across the entrance of the sheepfold at night, literally becoming the door — no sheep could enter or leave without passing over him. Jesus takes this image and declares himself the only legitimate access to God’s people and God’s salvation. “He will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture” — salvation in John is not merely rescue from judgment but entry into the abundant life of the flock: community, nourishment, freedom, the presence of the Shepherd. “I came that they may have life and have it abundantly” (v. 10) is John’s summary of the Gospel. Not bare survival but overflowing life.

verseByVerse.quote: All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The claim that all who came before Jesus are thieves and robbers is not a comprehensive condemnation of the Old Testament prophets (Jesus explicitly cites them as witnesses to himself) but an indictment of the false claimants to messianic authority and the leaders who have exercised authority over Israel's flock for self-advancement rather than the flock's welfare. The prophets themselves made exactly this critique of Israel's shepherds (Ezek 34; Zech 11:15-17): God's appointed shepherds repeatedly became exploiters. Jesus stands in contrast to this pattern: he is both the door through which legitimate access comes and the shepherd who gives his life for the sheep. The sheep's not listening to the thieves — they did not listen to them — is the mark of genuine faith: the sheep recognise the true shepherd's voice and flee the voice of strangers.

verseByVerse.quote: The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly.
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast between theft/destruction and abundant life is one of the most quoted verses in John's Gospel, and its context is crucial: Jesus is defining his mission in contrast to every false shepherd, every religious leader who has used the flock for his own benefit. The abundant life (zōē perisson — life in superabundance) is not merely eternal life in the future but a quality of life in the present that exceeds what the thief could ever provide. Carson notes that the abundance is not a prosperity promise but the overflowing of the divine life into human existence — the life of the one in whom life itself dwells (1:4), poured out through the death that the good shepherd is about to describe. The thief and the shepherd define two ways of relating to God's people: exploitation and sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The fourth “I AM” statement. The adjective “good” (kalos) means not merely morally good but beautiful, genuine, noble — the shepherd who perfectly embodies what a shepherd should be. The defining characteristic is self-sacrifice: “lays down his life for the sheep.” The Greek is striking — tithenai tēn psychēn, literally “to place down his soul.” This is not accidental death or martyrdom forced upon him; it is a deliberate, chosen act of surrender. Verse 18 makes it explicit: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord.” The cross in John is not tragedy; it is the supreme act of the shepherd’s love, freely chosen, on behalf of the sheep who could not save themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them. He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep.
verseByVerse.commentary: The hired hand is a third figure in the parable, between the thief and the good shepherd: not actively malicious but not genuinely invested. His care extends only as far as the payment that motivates it; when cost exceeds benefit (the wolf arrives), he abandons the flock. The contrast with the good shepherd — who lays down his life — could not be starker. The hired hand is the image of ministry without genuine love: technically present, procedurally correct, but fundamentally self-serving. The Reformers read this passage as a challenge to institutional religion that cares more for its own preservation than for the souls under its care. Genuine pastoral ministry, modelled on the good shepherd, is characterised by the willingness to absorb cost rather than transfer it.

verseByVerse.quote: “I know my own and my own know me, just as the Father knows me and I know the Father.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The mutual knowledge of shepherd and sheep is grounded in and modelled on the mutual knowledge of Father and Son. This is one of the most extraordinary analogies in Scripture: the intimacy of the eternal Trinitarian relationship — Father knowing Son, Son knowing Father in perfect, infinite, mutual love — is the pattern for the intimacy between Christ and his people. “Knowing” in this context is not mere intellectual awareness but the covenantal knowledge of love, commitment, and presence. To be known by Jesus is to be known as he knows the Father: completely, unchangeably, with a love that will not let go.

verseByVerse.quote: And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd.
verseByVerse.commentary: The other sheep not of this fold are the Gentiles — those outside the covenant of Israel who will hear the shepherd's voice and be brought in. The one flock, one shepherd is the eschatological vision of a unified people of God drawn from all nations, with a single shepherd rather than the divided flock of competing religious systems. The must (dei) of bringing them is the same divine necessity that governs Jesus's entire mission: it is not merely possible for Gentiles to be included but ordained by the Father. This verse is the missiological heart of John 10 and grounds the later Gentile mission theologically: the good shepherd is gathering his scattered sheep from every fold, and the gospel's geographic expansion is the enacted fulfilment of this promise.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again.
verseByVerse.commentary: The authority of the good shepherd over his own death is one of the most theologically important statements in the Gospel: the crucifixion is not a tragedy imposed from outside but an act of self-giving that Jesus undertakes voluntarily, with full authority to lay down his life and to take it up again. This is the divine ground of the resurrection: the same authority that enables the self-surrender enables the self-restoration. The division this statement produces among the Jews mirrors the division throughout the Gospel: some say he has a demon; others say no one who has a demon can open the eyes of the blind. The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) provides the setting for the final question — if you are the Christ, tell us plainly — and Jesus's response: I told you, and you do not believe. The works he does in the Father's name are the testimony; those who are not his sheep cannot hear his voice.

verseByVerse.quote: “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The most complete statement of the eternal security of believers in John. Three verbs, three negatives, two hands. The sheep hear, they know, they follow — and the result is: eternal life given, never perishing, no snatching out of his hand, no snatching out of the Father’s hand. The security rests not on the sheep’s grip on the Shepherd but on the Shepherd’s grip on the sheep — and behind that, on the Father’s grip, which is greater still. This is the Johannine equivalent of Romans 8:38–39: nothing in all creation shall separate us from the love of God in Christ. The security of the believer is as strong as the omnipotent hands of the Father and the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: “I and the Father are one.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The Greek hen (one) is neuter — not “one person” (heis) but “one thing,” one in nature, will, and action. This is not modalism (collapsing Father and Son into one person) but the assertion of essential unity. His opponents understand it as a claim to deity and reach for stones (v. 31) — the third time in John someone has tried to stone him for blasphemy. Jesus does not correct them by saying “I only meant we’re united in purpose”; he defends the claim from Scripture (Ps 82:6) while reaffirming that the Father is in him and he is in the Father (v. 38). “I and the Father are one” is the ontological foundation for every pastoral promise in the chapter: the security of the sheep rests on the unity of the Son with the omnipotent Father.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews picked up stones again to stone him... Jesus answered them, 'Is it not written in your Law, I said, you are gods? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came — and Scripture cannot be broken — do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, You are blaspheming?'
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus's argument from Psalm 82:6 — if Scripture calls human judges 'gods' because the word of God came to them, how much more can the one whom the Father himself sent into the world use divine language without blasphemy? — is a lesser-to-greater argument (qal wahomer) in the rabbinic style. It does not prove that Jesus is merely human; it rather shows that the accusation of blasphemy is disproportionate even on their own reading of Scripture. The works he does are the ultimate proof: if you do not believe me, believe the works. Jesus's escape from their attempt to arrest him and his withdrawal across the Jordan, where many believed in him, brings the Book of Signs (John 1-12) toward its midpoint with a summary: John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true, and many believed in him there.

10.theology: The eternal security of the elect. John 10:27–29 is the strongest New Testament statement of what Reformed theology calls the perseverance of the saints — or more precisely, the preservation of the saints by God. The grounds for security are entirely outside the believer: eternal life is given (not achieved), the sheep will never perish (the negation is absolute in Greek: ou mē — never, ever), and no one can snatch them (the passive construction places the power of keeping entirely in the Shepherd’s hands). The Arminian reading — that the sheep can choose to leave the fold of their own accord — is not exegetically available from this text. The promise is not “no external force can remove you” but “you will never perish” — an absolute guarantee of final perseverance rooted in the omnipotent love of the triune God.
10.examples:
Then: Ezekiel 34 pronounced judgment on Israel’s shepherds who fed themselves rather than the flock, who ruled harshly, who let the sheep scatter. God promised: “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep” (Ezek 34:15). Jesus stands in the temple courts and announces that promise fulfilled. The good shepherd has arrived. The sheep who were scattered are being gathered. The false shepherds who cast out the healed man are exposed for what they are.

Now: “No one will snatch them out of my hand” is the pastoral anchor for every believer in every storm. Not the storm of doubt, not the storm of sin, not the storm of suffering, not the storm of persecution. The shepherd’s hands are the Father’s hands. No one is stronger. The sheep may wander; the shepherd goes after them (Luke 15). The sheep may stumble; the shepherd carries them (Isa 40:11). The shepherd’s grip does not depend on the sheep’s grip. It never did.

11.title: The Resurrection and the Life
11.text: <sup>21</sup>Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. <sup>23</sup>Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.” <sup>24</sup>Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.” <sup>25</sup>Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, <sup>26</sup>and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?” <sup>27</sup>She said to him, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.” <sup>33</sup>When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews also weeping who had come with her, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. <sup>35</sup>Jesus wept. <sup>43</sup>When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.” <sup>44</sup>The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Unbind him, and let him go.” <sup>53</sup>So from that day on they made plans to put him to death.
11.overview:
Chapter 11 is the summit of John’s signs and the hinge of the entire Gospel. The raising of Lazarus — dead four days, already decaying — is the seventh and greatest sign, the one that makes the resurrection of Jesus credible and that makes the crucifixion of Jesus inevitable. The Sanhedrin’s meeting in verses 47–53 is explicit: because of Lazarus, Jesus must die. The sign that demonstrates his power over death is the one that seals his death sentence. John’s theology of glory and suffering, exaltation and crucifixion, is nowhere more visible than here.

At the centre of the chapter stands the fifth “I AM” statement: “I am the resurrection and the life.” Martha confesses belief in a future resurrection; Jesus corrects her eschatological tense — the resurrection is not only a future event; he is the resurrection, present now, in this garden, outside this tomb. The one who stands before the sealed stone is the one in whom all resurrection life is located. He does not go to a place called resurrection; he brings resurrection wherever he goes. And then — before the miracle — the shortest and most theologically dense verse in Scripture: “Jesus wept.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha... So the sisters sent to him, saying, 'Lord, he whom you love is ill.' But when Jesus heard it he said, 'This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and greatest sign in John's Gospel, and its narrative preparation is the longest of any sign: twenty-seven verses before the miracle, building expectation and theological depth. Jesus's delay upon hearing of Lazarus's illness — he stayed two more days — is not indifference but the same divine timing that governed every other moment in the Gospel. His statement — this illness does not lead to death — turns out to be true in the deepest sense, even though Lazarus does die: death is not the final word. The disciples' misunderstanding of Lazarus's sleeping and Jesus's explicit statement — Lazarus has died — followed by I am glad for your sake that I was not there, so that you may believe — reveal Jesus's comprehensive perspective on the event: what looks like tragedy is the occasion for the most revealing sign. Thomas's come, that we may die with him is both darkly humorous and prophetically true.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days... Martha said to Jesus, 'Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Martha's two-part statement — if you had been here, he would not have died; even now God will give you whatever you ask — is a confession of faith that is simultaneously complete and incomplete. She believes in Jesus's power to heal the living; she is about to discover his power over the dead. Her faith is genuine but bounded by her eschatological category: she knows Lazarus will rise in the resurrection at the last day. Jesus's I am the resurrection and the life is not a correction but an expansion: the resurrection she is waiting for at the last day is present now, in Jesus himself. The last day is not delayed; it has begun. Whoever believes in him, though he die, yet shall he live; whoever lives and believes in him shall never die. Two promises: the dead who believe will live again; the living who believe will never ultimately die.

verseByVerse.quote: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The fifth “I AM” statement is also the most existentially urgent. Martha is standing outside her brother’s tomb, four days into grief. Jesus does not offer comfort, philosophy, or a theological lecture; he makes a claim about himself. He is not the agent of resurrection (as if he performed it on behalf of someone else); he is the resurrection itself. All resurrection life is located in his person. “Though he die, yet shall he live” — physical death is not the end for those who are united to the one who is life. “Everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die” — the second clause addresses those still alive: spiritual death, the second death, the death that is separation from God — that death has no power over those who are in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Martha’s confession is the Johannine equivalent of Peter’s at Caesarea Philippi (Matt 16:16) — and John places it at the theological centre of the Gospel. She confesses three titles: the Christ (the Messiah of Israel’s hope), the Son of God (his divine identity), and “the one coming into the world” (the fulfilment of all eschatological expectation). She makes this confession standing outside a tomb, in the midst of grief, without yet seeing the miracle. This is faith before the evidence, faith in the person before the performance — which is why John records it here. The miracle confirms the confession; the confession does not wait for the miracle.

verseByVerse.quote: When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, 'The Teacher is here and is calling for you.' And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him... When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled.
verseByVerse.commentary: Mary's response — falling at Jesus's feet, the posture of worship and supplication — and her identical words to her sister (if you had been here, my brother would not have died) show the depth of shared grief and the same limitation of faith. The difference is that Mary comes in tears rather than theological conversation, and Jesus's response to her weeping is different from his response to Martha's words: he is deeply moved (embrimaomai — a word suggesting strong emotion, possibly indignation at death's power) and troubled. Verse 35 — Jesus wept — is the shortest verse in Scripture and one of the most theologically significant: God incarnate weeps at a human grave. The one who is about to demonstrate his authority over death grieves at its presence. This is not contradiction but incarnation: Jesus's power over death does not immunise him from feeling its horror.

verseByVerse.quote: “Jesus wept.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The shortest verse in the Bible contains one of its most profound theological statements. The eternal Son of God, who knows he is about to raise Lazarus, who knows that death has no final power over those who are his — he weeps. Not for Lazarus (who is about to be raised) but with Mary and the mourners, entering into the reality of their grief. This is the empathy of the incarnation: he does not stand above human sorrow with omniscient detachment; he enters it, is “deeply moved” (embrimaomai — a word of intense inner agitation, almost anger at death’s intrusion), and weeps. The one who is the resurrection feels the weight of death. He will bear that weight to the cross. The tears at Lazarus’ tomb are a sign of what the cross will cost.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said, 'See how he loved him!' But some of them said, 'Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?' And Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
verseByVerse.commentary: The crowd's division — some who see in Jesus's tears evidence of love, others who see in Lazarus's death evidence of limitation — is John's consistent depiction of the same event producing opposite interpretations. The mention of the opened blind man's eyes (chapter 9) links the two great sign narratives: the sign of giving sight to the blind is now recalled as evidence of capacity; the question is whether that capacity extends to the dead. Jesus's prayer before the open tomb is unique in the Gospel: he thanks the Father for hearing him, and then explains that he is not praying for the Father's benefit but for the crowd's benefit — so that they may believe that you sent me. The prayer is itself a sign: a public declaration of the relationship between Father and Son that grounds the miracle in the Father's eternal will rather than the Son's independent action.

verseByVerse.quote: “Lazarus, come out.” The man who had died came out.
verseByVerse.commentary: Calvin observed that Jesus called Lazarus by name — otherwise, all the dead might have come out. The particularity of the call is the point: the good shepherd calls his own sheep by name (10:3), and the dead hear the voice of the Son of God and live (5:25). “Lazarus, come out” is the pattern of the final resurrection, enacted now in one tomb outside Bethany. The bound man comes out — and Jesus says “unbind him.” The resurrection body is free; it is the grave-clothes of the old life that must be removed. This is a pastoral charge to the community: the work of resurrection belongs to Christ; the work of unbinding belongs to the church, as we help one another to walk free from what once bound us.

verseByVerse.quote: Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him, but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.
verseByVerse.commentary: The division after the greatest sign is the sharpest in the Gospel: many believe; some report to the Pharisees. The most dramatic demonstration of Jesus's identity — the raising of a man four days dead — produces the same two responses as every previous sign. The reporting to the Pharisees is not necessarily malicious; they may have been genuinely uncertain what to make of what they saw. But the Sanhedrin's response (vv.47-53) will turn their report into the catalyst for the decision to arrest and kill Jesus. The irony is complete: the sign that most clearly demonstrates Jesus as the resurrection and the life provokes the decision that will lead to his own death — a death that, as Caiaphas unwittingly prophesies, will be for the whole nation.

verseByVerse.quote: “It is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Caiaphas’ speech is the most ironic moment in John’s Gospel. He intends a cynical political calculation: sacrifice one man to protect the nation from Roman reprisal. John reads it as unwitting prophecy: “he did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad” (vv. 51–52). The greatest sign provokes the definitive decision: “from that day on they made plans to put him to death.” The resurrection of Lazarus is the immediate cause of the crucifixion of Jesus. The one who gives life will die so that others might live. Caiaphas says it without knowing it. John says it knowing everything.

verseByVerse.quote: He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.
verseByVerse.commentary: John's editorial comment on Caiaphas's prophecy — he did not say this of his own accord — is one of the most striking instances in the Gospel of divine speech through unwitting human instruments. The high priest, motivated entirely by political calculation (better that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish), articulates the theological truth of the atonement without intending to. The gathering of the scattered children of God from every nation is the scope of Christ's death: not merely an expiation for Israel but for the dispersed children of God across the world. This verse is John's own commentary on the work of Christ — substitutionary, effective, universal in scope — embedded in the narrative of the decision to kill him. The irony is complete: the very council that condemns him pronounces his saving purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples. Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus's withdrawal to Ephraim is the last quiet moment before the Passion week begins. The Passover drawing near creates the temporal frame: the one who is the lamb of God (1:29) will be crucified at the Passover, when the lambs are slaughtered. The crowds coming to Jerusalem for the feast are speculating about whether Jesus will appear — there was a command from the chief priests and Pharisees that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know. The whole city is watching, waiting, and divided. Jesus's hour is about to arrive, and everything in the narrative has been building toward it. The withdrawal to Ephraim is not flight but preparation; when the hour comes, Jesus will not be taken by surprise but will enter Jerusalem on his own terms, at his own time, with the sovereign intentionality that has characterised his entire ministry.

11.theology: Christ as the resurrection and the life. John 11:25 is the fifth “I AM” statement and the most eschatologically dense. Reformed theology has always insisted that resurrection is not merely a future event to be waited for but a present reality to be participated in through union with Christ. Paul says we have been “raised with Christ” (Col 3:1); John says the one who believes in the Son “has passed from death to life” (5:24). The full, bodily resurrection at the last day is the consummation of a union that already exists. Because Christ is the resurrection — because all resurrection life is located in his person — those who are in him already possess eternal life, even though they will still die physically and be raised bodily at the end. The tomb at Bethany is a foretaste of the empty tomb in Jerusalem three weeks later.
11.examples:
Then: Mary and Martha both said the same words to Jesus when he arrived: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (vv. 21, 32). The rebuke in the sentence is palpable: you came too late. Jesus did not come too late; he came exactly on time. The four days were necessary so that no one could claim Lazarus had merely been in a coma. The delay was not absence; it was preparation for a greater glory. Every Christian who has prayed and not received the answer when they expected it is standing with Mary and Martha at the tomb.

Now: “Jesus wept” is the pastoral text for Christian grief. Christians grieve (1 Thess 4:13 does not say “you will not grieve”) — but not as those without hope. The tears of Jesus at the tomb of Lazarus sanctify our tears. He is not embarrassed by our weeping; he joins it. And he joins it as the one who is the resurrection and the life — which means that while we weep at the tomb, we weep with one who has already secured what the tomb cannot hold. Grief and hope are not opposites; they are the two notes of the Christian’s lament.

12.title: The Hour Has Come
12.text: <sup>3</sup>Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. <sup>12</sup>The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. <sup>13</sup>So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!” <sup>23</sup>And Jesus answered them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. <sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. <sup>31</sup>Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out. <sup>32</sup>And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” <sup>46</sup>I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. <sup>47</sup>If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world.
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is the great transition of John’s Gospel — the hinge between the Book of Signs (chapters 1–12) and the Book of Glory (chapters 13–21).
